original_misconception.description: Student believes that while loops execute their body only once if the condition is true.

predicted_misconceptions.explanation:
In each of the first four student programs the while loop’s control variable (i or pembagi) is never updated inside the loop body.  
- In Code 1 the loop that scans the string never increments i, so the condition `i <= panjang(s) - 2` remains true forever.  
- In Code 2 the loop that tests divisors never increments pembagi, causing an infinite loop.  
- In Code 3 the loop that sums the harmonic series never decrements i, so the loop never terminates.  
- In Code 4 the loop that reads words never increments i, again leading to an infinite loop.  

The reference solutions all include the necessary increment (`i <- i + 1` or `pembagi <- pembagi + 1`) inside the loop body. This pattern shows a consistent misconception that the loop control variable is automatically updated, which is not true in the Notasi Algoritmik pseudocode.  
Code 5, while using a while loop, does not exhibit this issue because the loop condition depends on a different variable (hasil) that is changed inside the loop, but the shared misconception across the other samples is the failure to update the loop counter.

original_misconception.description: Student believes that a variable assigned an arithmetic expression containing other variables automatically updates its value when those variables change.

predicted_misconceptions.description: The student believes that assigning a variable to another variable creates a dynamic link so that subsequent changes to the original variable automatically update the assigned variable.
predicted_misconceptions.explanation:
In all five student programs the same false belief appears.  
In Code 1 the student writes  
```  
terkecil <- x  
hasil <- terkecil  
```  
and later changes `terkecil` inside the loop, but never updates `hasil`.  
The program therefore outputs the initial value of `hasil` instead of the new minimum.  
The same pattern occurs in Code 2, where `panjangMax` is set once and never updated when new words are read; the student expects the earlier assignment to keep `panjangMax` linked to the current word length.  
In Code 3 the variable `hasil` is intended to hold the smallest value, yet it is never reassigned after `terkecil` changes.  
Code 4 assigns `hasilBalik` once before the loop that changes `kandidat`; the student expects `hasilBalik` to automatically recompute when `kandidat` changes.  
Finally, Code 5 pre‑computes `indeksBerikut` and `indeksBerikut2` once and then uses them in the loop, assuming they will automatically refer to the next characters as `i` increments.  

All these examples show the same misconception: the student thinks that once a variable is assigned the value of another variable, the two remain linked and any later change to the original variable will be reflected in the assigned variable. In the pseudocode language used, assignments copy the value, not create a reference, so the assigned variable must be updated explicitly whenever the original changes.

predicted_misconceptions.description: The student believes that a loop counter variable can be reused for other purposes inside the loop or after the loop without affecting the loop control or the program’s logic.
predicted_misconceptions.explanation:
All five student programs exhibit this belief.  
In Code 1 the loop counter `n` is used as the loop variable (`for n <- 1 to n do`) and then later as the upper bound, which changes the loop’s behavior.  
Code 2 introduces a second loop `for hasil <- 1 to n do` that merely assigns `minimum <- minimum`; the variable `hasil` is also used later to store the final result, overwriting the loop counter.  
Code 3 sets `i <- 100` before the loop and then reuses `i` as the loop counter (`for i <- 1 to n do`), but finally outputs `i` instead of the intended `terkecil`.  
Code 4 uses `i` as the loop counter and then checks `if i == 0` after the loop, assuming `i` would still hold the initial value.

In each case the student treats the loop variable as a general-purpose variable, ignoring that its value is controlled by the loop construct and that reassigning it can corrupt the loop’s intended iteration or the program’s final result. This misconception leads to incorrect logic and, in some cases, to runtime errors or wrong outputs.
